title: Theory-agnostic nonclassicality certification in an integrated photonic circuit
authors: Vinicius P. Rossi, Emanuele Polino, Beatrice Polacchi, Valeria Cimini, David Schmid, John H. Selby, Giacomo Corrielli, Andrea Crespi, Roberto Osellame, Fabio Sciarrino, Ana Belén Sainz
abstract: Certifying nonclassicality without assuming any particular underlying physical theory constitutes both a foundational challenge and a requirement for device-independent protocols. Realizing such theory-independent certification in scalable architectures is essential for connecting fundamental tests with emerging quantum technologies. Integrated photonic circuits are a leading platform for scalable quantum information processing, motivating the development of rigorous methods to certify the nonclassical resources underpinning quantum advantage. In this paper, we report a theory-independent certification of generalized contextuality on a three-mode integrated photonic circuit. Our approach combines theory-agnostic tomography with simplex-embeddability certification---a framework that requires no assumptions about the underlying physical theory---and applies it to experimental data from a three-mode photonic circuit seeded by single photons. An independently constructed quantum model of the experiment provides a consistency check on the observed nonclassicality, without entering the certification as a theoretical assumption. The method rules out simplex-embeddability for our experimental data, providing robust, theory-independent evidence that our photonic circuit exhibits nonclassicality.
summary: This paper presents a theory-agnostic method to certify nonclassicality using only experimental statistics from an integrated photonic circuit. By combining theory-agnostic tomography with simplex-embeddability certification, the authors robustly demonstrate that the measured correlations cannot be explained by any classical physical model. This advances the field by providing a general, device-independent verification tool for quantum advantage in scalable photonic platforms.
main_problem: The paper addresses the foundational challenge of certifying nonclassicality in a manner that is independent of any specific underlying physical theory, which is vital for device-independent quantum protocols.
main_result: The authors successfully applied a theory-agnostic certification method to experimental data from a three-mode integrated photonic circuit, providing robust evidence of nonclassicality by ruling out simplex-embeddability.
method: The core method combines theory-agnostic tomography with simplex-embeddability certification, which analyzes experimental statistics to determine the minimal mathematical structure (rank) required to explain the observed correlations.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes a three-mode integrated photonic circuit, operating in a prepare-and-measure scenario, where quantum correlations are generated and measured using single photons.
key_observables: The primary observable is the conditional probability distribution $p(a|y, x)$, and the diagnostic tools are the optimal factorization rank ($k^*$) and the robustness of contextuality ($r$).
important_parameters: The analysis depends on the measured coincidence counts ($N$) and the independently controlled voltages ($\Delta V_x, \Delta V_y$) used to tune the photonic circuit settings.
main_assumptions: The method's strength lies in its minimal assumptions, but limitations include the fact that the reconstructed fragments are 'GPT shadows' and the complexity of polytope representation growth.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual setup (prepare-and-measure), the measured/modeled probabilities as functions of applied voltages, and comparisons of robustness ($r$) and $\chi^2$ values for classical versus theoretical models.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory-agnostic framework by defining the optimization problem ($\chi^2$ minimization over rank $k$), applies it to the photonic circuit data, and validates the procedure by comparing results against known classical and theoretical quantum models.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general mathematical tool for verifying quantum resources directly from measurements, which is highly relevant for assessing the performance and fundamental limits of photonic quantum hardware.

Figure 3 summarises the results for (A–B) the theoretical model and (C–D) the experimental data. Figs. 3-A and 3-C show how χ2 train and χ2 test change with the rank k assumed for the factorization of the data table. One can see that the assumption of k = 4 yields a much larger value for both χ2 train and χ2 test, which quickly collapses for k = 5. This holds for both the theoretical probabilities and the experimental data.
